abstract: Hot-wire icing probes infer cloud water content from heating power, but under-read systematically because impacting droplets splash and shed. Correcting for this retention deficit requires a calibrated retention efficiency curve, and that curve is only as trustworthy as the statistical procedure behind it. This paper documents the methodology used to calibrate retention efficiency for five sensor elements against an isokinetic reference probe in an icing research tunnel. Key methodological contributions include: a multi-criteria procedure that auditably selects between a linear and a piece-wise retention model by requiring unanimous agreement among an F-test, a breakpoint-stability test, and the Bayesian Information Criterion; a hybrid uncertainty propagation scheme that dispatches to Monte Carlo near the model breakpoint where an analytic Taylor expansion fails; and a four-axis condition match to pair the two instruments. Of the five elements, two resolve a genuine retention breakpoint, one is cleanly linear, and two are indeterminate. The methodology prioritizes auditable decision-making, detailing the iterative corrections required to prevent artifactual curve fits.
title: Auditable Model Selection and Hybrid Uncertainty Propagation for Hot-Wire Icing Retention Efficiency

abstract: NASA's independent validation that an agentic AI approach to ML development can match or exceed expert-crafted predictive models for departure runway prediction in the National Airspace System. The study benchmarks NASA's Agentic AI platform — which autonomously executes the full ML lifecycle including feature discovery, model selection, and hyperparameter optimization via LLM-driven agents and Bayesian search — against legacy XGBoost models that were developed through years of direct collaboration with FAA Traffic Management Coordinators and validated in live NAS operations. Across five independent experiments at DFW and IAH using LightGBM classifiers, the agentic models achieved 86.5% accuracy at DFW (within 2.7 pp of the 89.2% legacy baseline) and 84.2% at IAH, a 2.6 pp improvement over the legacy 81.6%, including resolution of a known systematic misclassification of Runway 9 — driven by novel features (configuration change timestamps and estimated fix-crossing times) that the prior process had missed. The paper concludes that agentic ML development is faster, more reproducible, and scalable without proportional expert investment, and that all future NASA NAS predictive models will be built through this pipeline.
title: Agentic Machine Learning Development for Departure Runway Prediction in the National Airspace System

abstract:
What is MAUNA? MAUNA automates high-throughput spacecraft trajectory analysis by generating, executing, and post-processing thousands of General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT) propagations across multidimensional design spaces. This replaces manually created and modified scripts with a standardized, reproducible workflow and enables systematic exploration of large orbital trade spaces.

Where does AI/ML actually enter? Mauna-generated high-fidelity trajectory data provide a foundation for physics-informed machine learning. For lunar impact prediction, machine learning (ML) can learn the slow, long-term evolution of orbital states while known gravitational physics constrain the solution; trajectories are then returned to high-fidelity numerical propagation near the terminal event to accurately resolve the impact location.

What has NASA actually used this for / why does it matter? 
The framework has been applied to lunar mission-design problems supporting NASA’s Artemis HLS and CLPS programs, including high-fidelity low-lunar-orbit stability analysis, automated searches across hundreds of thousands of candidate trajectories, and mapping of natural impact/disposal behavior. This combination of automation, physics-based simulation, and ML enables faster identification of stable orbital regimes and potential surface-interaction risks.
subject_categories: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration
title: Mauna: Automating High Throughput Orbit Propagation for NASA Missions

abstract:
Accurate Eulerian prediction of flow over a porous matrix requires closure models for
fluid-solid momentum exchange that capture strong local spatial heterogeneities. Poreresolved
simulation data for flow through random sphere packings over a wide range of
global porosities and particle Reynolds numbers are used to assess local closures for drag
and subfilter stress by volume-filtering at scales proportional to particle size. Applying
the Tenneti correlation with local filtered porosity and Reynolds number produces substantial
local errors. Re-optimizing the correlation separately for each filter width reduces
the error at low and moderate Reynolds numbers, but provides limited improvement at
high Reynolds number and porosity, where local drag becomes increasingly non-collinear
with the filtered velocity. Application of the standard closure to turbulent flow over a
porous matrix also shows large deviations near the fluid-porous interface, but substantial
improvement is obtained when trained with data in the interfacial region. These results
indicate that local porosity and Reynolds number alone are insufficient for a general Eulerian
force closure and motivate investigation of additional directional descriptors of the
local flow and pore geometry. Finally, a nonlinear gradient Clark model provides good
prediction for the subfilter stress.
title: Volume Filtered Subgrid Closures for Upscaled Modeling of Flow in A Porous Matrix

abstract: Liquid Oxygen / Liquid Methane Confined-by-Missile (CBM) explosion type testing was conducted in collaboration by NASA Stennis Space Center,  NASA Marshall Space Flight Center Blast Team and Eglin Air Force Base.  The prompt-propagation tests of this test series was focused on evaluating the potential sympathetic detonation of liquid oxygen and liquid methane propellant tanks due to an explosion occurring immediately below the vertically stacked tanks.  This type of configuration and explosion would simulate an explosion originating from the engine area or perhaps a 1st stage in a multi-stage launch vehicle.  The additive explosive yield provided by the pre-unmixed propellants for both tank orientations was quantified.  The total propellant mass targeted for these tests was 100 lbm.   The explosions were initiated by 25 lbm of C-4 mounted on the base of the lower tank.   Blast wave over-pressure and high-speed video data collected during the test program were processed by the NASA led multi-agency data analysis team.  This document serves to provide a summary of the optimized data analysis produced and the resulting conclusions regarding the yields achieved during this test program.  Ultimately, this processed data package will serve to guide safety analyses for LOX/Methane launch vehicle failures occurring on the launch pad or test stand.
title: CBM 2 Prompt Propagation Tests Optimized Data Analysis (ODA)

abstract: Liquid Oxygen / Liquid Methane propellant reaction characterization (PRC) testing was conducted at the NASA White Sands Test Facility.  The PRC dewar tests utilized an array of glass dewars positioned inside a larger aluminum pan, where the dewars were filled with liquid oxygen (LOX) and the space surrounding the glass dewars inside the pan was filled with liquid methane (or LNG).   The dewars were broken by command detonation of an explosive detonating cord attached to the bottom of the LNG filled pan.  Through this configuration, it was desired to invoke rapid and large contact surface area between the two propellants, allow them to mix if possible and then either auto-ignite or force an ignition.   The ultimate goal was to understand the contribution of LOX/LNG yield in this distributed mixing scenario.  Key test parameters investigated were LNG purity, oxygen-to-fuel mass ratio and if possible ignition delay.  Blast wave over-pressure and high-speed video data collected during the test program were processed by the NASA led multi-agency data analysis team.  This document serves to provide a summary of the optimized data analysis produced and the resulting conclusions regarding the yields achieved during this test program.  Ultimately, this data package will serve to guide model development for safety analyses of LOX/Methane launch vehicles on a launch pad or test stand.
title: Propellant Reaction Characterization (PRC) Phase 1 (Dewar/Distributed Mixing) Tests Optimized Data Analysis (ODA)
Modeling the Orbital Debris Environment
